docs.title: PeekSeek
docs.text:
PeekSeek is an open-source matchmaking and esports platform. It runs peekseek.net for Unturned, and everything that makes it work is in one repository.

These docs are for three kinds of people:

  • You want to run your own instance. Start at Getting Started.
  • You want to understand how it works before trusting it. Start at Architecture.
  • You want it for a different game. Start at Forking. The part of the system that talks to game servers was built to not care what game it is.

docs.title: What it does
docs.text: Matchmaking Players queue, servers pull. Teams are balanced on Elo with a configurable gap, and a rematch cooldown stops the same two people meeting twice in a row. Match hosting A pool of game servers claims matches, runs them, and reports results back. Servers that go quiet are noticed. Lobbies A persistent arena players wait in, which queues them without leaving the game. Ranking Elo per player, adjusted from reported match results. Parties Queue together, stay together. Events Tournament pairings and signups on top of the same match machinery. Stream overlays A separate flat HUD any broadcaster can point OBS at. Discord A live player counter, queue logging, and a ping when a dead arena wakes up.

docs.title: The pieces
docs.text:
Four deployables, one repository. They share it because the site and the plugins are two halves of one contract, and a change to both belongs in one commit.

Component What it is Language website/ The whole site and API: pages, the JSON its own scripts call, and the /server/v1/* API game servers run on FastAPI, Python 3.12 plugins/peekseek/ Runs matches on a game server: match state, lifecycle, ping-based damage scaling C#, net48 plugins/peekseek-lobby/ Runs the waiting arena: queueing from in-game, kits, AFK handling C#, net48 plugins/utelemetry/ PvP telemetry beyond kill counts C#, net48

The two RocketMod plugins are the only Unturned-specific code in the system. The website never imports anything that knows what Unturned is.

docs.title: The one idea worth reading first
docs.text:
A match cannot exist without a game server holding it.

Matchmaking does not run when a player queues. Queueing only puts you in the queue. When a server reports itself free, that server's own poll scans the queue, forms the best match it can, and takes it, all before answering the request.

So a matchmade match is created already assigned to the server that will host it. There is no scheduler, no broker, and no window where a match exists with nowhere to play it. The match lifecycle walks through what that means in practice.

docs.title: Licence
docs.text: MIT, per LICENSE. Fork it, run it, sell it. Attribution is welcome and not required.

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text:
One FastAPI app serves three different audiences on one port. That is the whole shape of the system, and most of what follows is a consequence of it.

Audience Gets Authenticated by People Server-rendered Jinja pages Steam or Discord login, signed session cookie The site's own scripts JSON endpoints The same session cookie Game servers /server/v1/* The caller's source IP, allow-listed

docs.title: Layout
docs.text:
website/
├── public/                # served at /static
│   ├── assets/css/        # one stylesheet per page, plus default.css for the shared parts
│   ├── assets/js/         # one script per page
│   └── img/ maps/ unturned/
└── src/
    ├── app.py             # assembly: middleware, routers, error pages
    ├── dependencies.py    # current user, auth guards, template renderer
    ├── config.toml        # non-secret settings
    ├── kits.json          # kit catalog
    ├── mmconfig.json      # gamemode definitions
    ├── core/              # domain logic: settings, db, models, matchmaking, steam
    ├── routes/            # one APIRouter per area
    ├── templates/         # Jinja2 pages
    └── tests/

core/ is where behaviour lives. routes/ is thin on purpose: a route reads a request, calls into core/, and renders. There is no utils.py, and adding one would be a regression.

docs.title: The two authentication systems
docs.text:
They have nothing in common and that is intentional.

People log in through Steam or Discord and carry a signed session cookie. Permissions are bits on the user row, named in [permissions].list in config.toml, so the order of that list is a storage format and not a preference.

Game servers are recognised by source IP, from the AuthorizedServers table. Every route under /server/v1 returns 401 to an address that is not in it, and nothing in the site adds one. You seed the first entries with BOOTSTRAP_SERVERS.

Reverse proxies and --forwarded-allow-ips

Because server auth trusts request.client.host, uvicorn's proxy-header handling has to be scoped. Setting --forwarded-allow-ips=* means any caller can set X-Forwarded-For to an allow-listed address and walk through the IP check. The shipped Dockerfile scopes it to private ranges so only the proxy's own hop is trusted. Keep that property if you change the deployment.

docs.title: Data
docs.text:
SQLModel over SQLAlchemy, and DB takes any SQLAlchemy URL.

There is no migration tool. On startup, create_all builds tables that do not exist, and then addMissingColumns in src/core/db.py adds columns the models have gained since their table was built, backfilling a model default where there is one. Every ALTER it runs is printed at startup.

What that covers, and what it does not:

Change Handled New table Yes New column Yes, backfilled from the model default Dropped, renamed or retyped column No. Do it against the database by hand.

This is a deliberate trade. It means a new SQLModel table reaches production by being deployed, with no migration step to forget. It also means destructive schema changes are manual, on purpose.

docs.title: Configuration splits by kind, not by environment
docs.text:
• src/config.toml holds everything non-secret: matchmaking timings, gamemode names, permission bits, Discord channel ids, the lobby's connect code. Humans tune it and it is in the repository.
  • The environment holds secrets, plus three overrides (DOMAIN, PROTOCOL, BUILD) so one image can serve both dev and production.
  • kits.json and mmconfig.json hold machine-shaped datasets that are too big and too structured to read as TOML.

Everything funnels through one Settings object in src/core/settings.py. Nothing reads os.environ directly, and nothing hardcodes a value that already lives in config.

docs.title: Third parties never hold a page open
docs.text:
Steam is on the request path of pages that have to render without it, so every call into it is treated as decoration:

  • Lookups are cached, including failures, so an outage costs one request per cache window rather than one per item per page.
  • Server.describe does not call Steam at all. It answers from cache and fills the cache on a background thread, because the admin list asks about every match on it one after another, and a blocking miss multiplies by however many servers are on screen.
  • Player names and avatars are persisted on the user row when they are fetched, so an ordinary page never has to ask.

If you add a third-party call, match this. A page that renders slowly because a vendor is slow is a page that goes down when the vendor does.

docs.title: Front end
docs.text:
Server-rendered Jinja, one stylesheet and one script per page, plus HTMX where a partial update is worth it. There is no build step for the application code and no framework.

The only build-time transformation is minify.py, which compresses public/assets in place during the Docker build. The repository keeps readable source, the image serves compressed files, and no template has to know which build it is in. The compressors are uninstalled in the same layer and never reach the running container.

One consequence worth knowing

Because CSS is concatenated per file and served as written, plain cascade rules apply. Utility classes such as .hidden have to come last in a stylesheet to beat component rules of equal specificity.

docs.title: Overlays
docs.text: The stream overlay is a separate visual system from the site: flat greyscale, built to be legible over gameplay in OBS, not to match the site's branding. It is served by the same app at /overlay and reads the same match data. Treat it as a second product with a second design language rather than a themed page.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
Configuration splits by kind, not by environment.

Where Holds In the repository src/config.toml Everything non-secret Yes Environment Secrets, plus three per-deployment overrides No kits.json, mmconfig.json Machine-shaped datasets too structured for TOML Yes

Everything funnels through one Settings object in src/core/settings.py. Nothing reads os.environ directly, and nothing hardcodes a value that already lives in config. If you add a setting, add it there.

docs.title: Environment
docs.text:
Only DB is enforced at startup. Everything else is optional in code, and the features that depend on it no-op when it is missing. That is what lets a staging deployment run without the ability to touch anything real.

Variable Missing means DB The app will not start. Any SQLAlchemy URL. STEAM_API_KEY No persona names or avatars. Players still work, nameless. DISCORD_CLIENT_SECRET No Discord login. Steam login is unaffected. BOT_TOKEN No Discord player counter, and no channel renames. LOG_WEBHOOK No Discord logging. QUEUE_LOG_CHANNEL No queue logging. SECRET_KEY Session cookies are signed with the domain instead. Set this in production. DOMAIN Falls back to [app].domain. PROTOCOL Falls back to [app].protocol. BUILD Falls back to [app].build. BOOTSTRAP_ADMIN_STEAM64 No admin is created. A fresh database then has none. BOOTSTRAP_SERVERS No game server can authenticate.

Both bootstraps should be unset once they have done their job. See Self-hosting.

docs.title: [app]
docs.text:
[app]
domain = "127.0.0.1"   # public hostname, no scheme
protocol = "http"
build = "develop"

All three are overridable from the environment so one image can serve every deployment. Everything else in config.toml is the same everywhere.

docs.title: [matchmaking]
docs.text:
Every number that decides whether a roster becomes a match.

Key Default What it does queue_timeout 60 Seconds without a heartbeat before a player drops from the queue host_grace 20 Seconds past selection a serverless match waits before it is cancelled party_timeout 600 Seconds with nobody looking at a party before it disbands max_team_elo_gap 200 Widest average-Elo gap allowed between the two teams rematch_cooldown 300 Seconds before the same two players can be put against each other again

See the match lifecycle for how the last two interact. One repeated pairing rejects a whole roster.

docs.title: [lobby]
docs.text:
[lobby]
connect_code = "85568392936415589"

The server code /lobby hands to the game. This is the steamID64 the server's login token owns, so it survives restarts.

Store the code, never the address

A server running with FakeIP protection is given a fresh 169.254.x.x:port by Steam's relay every session, so the address is worth nothing written down. The code beside it in the server console changes only when the login token does.

Read a new one off the console after a token change. It is the line beginning Server Code:.

docs.title: [permissions]
docs.text:
[permissions]
list = ["admin", "canWriteBlog", "premium"]

Order is a storage format

A permission's index in this list is its bit in Users.permissions. Reordering the list silently reassigns everyone's permissions. Append only.

docs.title: [discord]
docs.text:
Key What it does client_id OAuth client id. Not a secret; the secret is DISCORD_CLIENT_SECRET. invite_url Where /discord redirects. counter_channel Voice channel renamed to the live player count. A channel id is not a secret. counter_interval Seconds between renames. Discord allows two per ten minutes and answers the third with a 429, so this cannot usefully go below ~300. wake_ping_after Seconds an arena must have been empty before the first player to walk in is worth announcing.

Nothing renames the channel unless BOT_TOKEN is set, which is what keeps a development instance from renaming the production one.

docs.title: [regions.names]
docs.text:
[regions.names]
paris = "EU-West"
utah = "US-West"
singapore = "AS-South"
brazil = "SA-East"

Region id on the left, display name on the right. The ids are what BOOTSTRAP_SERVERS assigns to each game server, and what matchmaking groups players by. Add a region here before allow-listing a server into it.

docs.title: [data_files]
docs.text:
Paths, relative to config.toml, of the two JSON datasets.

File Holds mmconfig.json Gamemode definitions: names, rounds, settings kits.json The kit catalogue: items, amounts, attachment state

These are JSON rather than TOML because they are machine-shaped: deep, repetitive, and edited by tooling more often than by hand. Both are the most game-specific files in the website, and the first two you replace when forking.

docs.title: Forking for another game
docs.text: PeekSeek runs Unturned, but very little of it knows that. This page is an honest inventory of what you would have to replace, ordered by how much work each part actually is.

docs.title: The part you get for free
docs.text:
/server/v1/* was built to not care what game it is. From API.md:

It is deliberately not Unturned-specific: a server for a different game implements the same calls and speaks the same JSON.

That is not aspiration. The website has no import, no branch and no model that reaches into Unturned. Matchmaking, Elo, parties, queueing, events, the admin panel, the stream overlay and the Discord integration are all game-agnostic already.

Your real job is writing one agent for your game that implements the polling loop. Everything below is smaller than that.

docs.title: What you actually write
docs.text:
A program that runs on your game server and does this:

  1. Poll GET /server/v1/session with serverCode and matchId.
  2. Switch on action: idle, wait, host, abort.
  3. On host, start a match from the payload: teams, per-player loadouts, settings.
  4. Stream POST /matches/{id}/kills and POST /matches/{id}/state as things happen.
  5. POST /matches/{id}/result at the end, retrying until acknowledged.

That is the entire contract. It is HTTP and JSON, so it can be a RocketMod plugin, a SourceMod extension, a Minecraft plugin, a sidecar process, or a few hundred lines in whatever language your game's modding API speaks.

Read the match lifecycle before you start. The retry semantics are the part people get wrong.

The two shipped plugins are the reference implementation:

Plugin Implements plugins/peekseek The match loop above plugins/peekseek-lobby The waiting arena, queueing from in-game, kits, AFK

docs.title: Layer 1: the launch link (an afternoon)
docs.text:
Unturned takes a server code on its launch command line, and there is no URL scheme that joins by code directly, so every join on the site goes through steam://run/<appid>.

The app id 304930 is currently hardcoded in four places:

File Line src/routes/pages.py UNTURNED_APP_ID src/templates/app/spectate.html twice, in the card link and the spectate button public/assets/js/admin.js the spectate button public/assets/js/match.js connectUrl()

If your game joins differently, this is where you change it. Lifting it into config.toml first is a good first commit for a fork, and a welcome pull request back.

docs.title: Layer 2: game data (a weekend)
docs.text:
Three things describe Unturned specifically. All are data, not code.

What Where Holds Kits src/kits.json Item ids, amounts, attachment state bytes Gamemodes src/mmconfig.json Modes, rounds to win, maps, per-mode settings Item metadata UnturnedItem in src/core/models/stat.py, table unturned_items Item names for display Assets public/unturned/, public/maps/ Icons and map images

The shapes are general. A "kit" is a list of things a player spawns with, and a "gamemode" is a named set of rules with a win condition. Whether an item id means an Unturned gun or a Counter-Strike weapon is not something the site inspects.

UnturnedItem is the one badly named table, since it is really "a display name for a game item". Renaming it is a schema change and therefore manual, per Architecture.

docs.title: Layer 3: identity (the real work)
docs.text:
This is the one to think about before starting.

PeekSeek identifies players by steam64, everywhere. It is the primary key on users, the id in every API payload, and the thing the login flow returns.

Coupling Why it exists steam64 as user id Unturned is a Steam game, so every player already has one Steam Web API Persona names and avatars Steam login One of the two supported sign-ins GSLT server codes How a server identifies itself and how players connect

If your game is on Steam, none of this is a problem. Change the app id and the game data, and you are done.

If it is not on Steam, you are replacing the identity layer. The site is helpful here in one specific way: steam64s are handled as strings throughout, precisely because they are 64-bit and JSON numbers are not. So the field is already an opaque string id, and substituting a different id scheme is less invasive than it sounds. Discord login already exists alongside Steam, which proves the user row does not truly require a Steam identity to be created.

Budget real time for it anyway. It touches the user model, both login flows, the API payloads and every template that renders a profile.

docs.title: What stays untouched
docs.text:
Worth stating plainly, because it is most of the value:

  • Matchmaking, Elo, and the balancing rules
  • Queueing, parties, and the rematch cooldown
  • The whole match lifecycle and its retry semantics
  • Events, signups, and tournament pairings
  • The admin panel
  • The stream overlay
  • Discord integration
  • Sessions, permissions, bans, and the IP allow-list

docs.title: A realistic order
docs.text:
1. Get the website running locally against SQLite. Getting Started.
  2. Read the match lifecycle until the retry rules make sense.
  3. Allow-list a machine you control with BOOTSTRAP_SERVERS and poll /server/v1/session by hand, with curl. You will see idle.
  4. Queue a player through the site and watch your poll turn into host.
  5. Only then write the game-side agent. By this point you know the contract.
  6. Swap the game data and the launch link.
  7. Replace identity, if your game is not on Steam.

Steps 3 and 4 are the ones people skip. They are also the ones that make the rest obvious.

docs.title: Contributing back
docs.text:
Fork-friendliness is a goal, so changes that reduce coupling are especially welcome: lifting the app id into config, generalising UnturnedItem, or anything that makes the identity layer pluggable.

See CONTRIBUTING.md for the branch model and conventions. The licence is MIT, so you owe nothing. It is just nicer this way.

docs.title: Getting Started
docs.text: This gets the website running on your machine with a throwaway database. You do not need a game server, and you do not need Unturned.

docs.title: What you need
docs.text:
• Python 3.12
  • Git

That is the whole list for a local site. Postgres is what production uses, but you can skip it for now.

docs.title: Run it
docs.text:
git clone https://github.com/PeekSeek/PeekSeek.git
cd PeekSeek/website
pip install -r requirements.txt
cp .env.example .env

Open .env and set one value:

DB=sqlite:////absolute/path/to/dev.db

Then start it:

uvicorn src.app:app --reload

The site is on localhost:8000. Interactive API docs, generated from the routes themselves, are at localhost:8000/docs.

SQLite is for convenience, not fidelity

DB takes any SQLAlchemy URL, and the schema is built by create_all either way. SQLite will not reproduce Postgres-specific problems, integer width being the obvious one. Use Postgres before you trust anything you measured.

docs.title: Make yourself an admin
docs.text:
A fresh database has no admin, and there is no way to promote the first one through the site. Set this in .env and restart once:

BOOTSTRAP_ADMIN_STEAM64=76561198000000000

It creates the account if it has never logged in. The Steam callback matches on steam64, so the row is reused at first login rather than duplicated. Leave it unset in production.

docs.title: What works without secrets
docs.text:
Most of it. Every integration no-ops on an empty value rather than crashing, which is deliberate: it is what lets the dev deployment run without the ability to touch anything real.

Unset What stops STEAM_API_KEY Persona names and avatars. Players still work, they are just nameless. DISCORD_CLIENT_SECRET Discord login. Steam login is unaffected. BOT_TOKEN The Discord player counter. LOG_WEBHOOK, QUEUE_LOG_CHANNEL Discord logging.

Pages backed by data render blank until something seeds them. That is an empty database, not a broken install.

docs.title: Run the tests
docs.text:
pytest -v

They use their own database and need no secrets, no network, and no game server. If they pass on a clean clone, your environment is fine.

docs.title: Build the plugins
docs.text:
Only if you have a game server to put them on.

cd plugins/peekseek          # or peekseek-lobby, or utelemetry
dotnet build PeekSeek.sln -c Release
dotnet test PeekSeek.sln

Builds pull the Rocket, Unturned and Unity assemblies from the RestoreMonarchy.RocketRedist NuGet package, so there are no hand-copied lib/ DLLs to find. The compiled DLL lands in plugin/bin/Release/net48/ and drops into the server's Rocket/Plugins/<name>/.

docs.title: The match lifecycle
docs.text:
If you read one page to understand the design, read this one. Every awkward-looking decision in the API comes from a single constraint.

The constraint

A match cannot exist without a game server holding it.

docs.title: Servers pull, they are never pushed
docs.text:
Matchmaking does not run when a player queues. Queueing only adds the player to the queue.

When a server reports itself free, that server's own poll scans the queue, forms the best match it can, and takes it, all before answering the request. A matchmade match is therefore created already assigned to the server that will host it.

The consequences are the whole point:

  • No scheduler and no broker to run or supervise.
  • No window where a match exists with nowhere to play it.
  • A server that dies simply stops polling. Nothing has to notice or reassign.
  • To add capacity you start a server. To remove it, you stop one.

Matches that players make for themselves, a custom match or an event pairing, are the exception. They do start with no server, and are handed to the next server that comes free. If none does before selection closes plus host_grace seconds, they are cancelled.

docs.title: The one call
docs.text:
A game server runs GET /server/v1/session on a loop, sending two things:

Parameter Meaning serverCode The code players connect with, the server's own Steam ID. 0 if it cannot report one. matchId The match it considers itself responsible for, including one it has finished but not yet successfully reported. 0 means free.

Exactly one of four answers comes back. action is the only field to switch on.

{"action": "idle"}
{"action": "wait",  "matchId": 42, "waitingOn": ["7656…"], "selectionEndsAt": 1786000060}
{"action": "host",  "match": { /* full payload */ }}
{"action": "abort", "matchId": 42, "reason": "matchOver"}
Answer Do idle Nothing. Ask again shortly. wait Hold the match, keep sending its matchId, let nobody in. The roster has not arrived yet. host Start it. Sent exactly once per match, so a slow poll cannot restart a round already being played. abort Drop it. reason is unknownMatch, matchOver or hostedElsewhere.

docs.title: Why the result report can be retried forever
docs.text:
A server that still names a match is never told that match was abandoned.

For as long as a server keeps saying "I am still holding match 42", the site will not decide match 42 was dropped. That single rule is what makes the result call safe to retry indefinitely, which matters because it is the only call that scores anything.

Route Retry Why POST /matches/{id}/state No Overlay snapshot. Each replaces the last, so a dropped one costs nothing. POST /matches/{id}/kills No One kill as it happens. Batching to the end loses the log with the server. POST /matches/{id}/result Yes, until acknowledged The only thing that scores a match.

The result answers {"status": "recorded"} or {"status": "alreadyRecorded"}. Repeats change nothing, so a reply lost on the way back costs a duplicate request rather than a doubled Elo swing. It is accepted even for a match already marked finished, because that is exactly what happens to a result that was slow to arrive.

Report the whole roster

players must include everyone on the match, including anyone who never joined and anyone who left. A player the server omits is a player whose Elo never moves, which is what used to make walking out of a losing match free.

played: false scores nothing and just releases the match. That is the honest answer when nobody turned up, and it is not the same as a real result that happened to be goalless.

docs.title: States
docs.text:
Derived from the match row rather than stored, so each fact lives in one place.

State Meaning pending Exists, no game server holds it. picking A server is holding it while its players choose. live Handed over. The server is running it. finished Scored, abandoned or cancelled. Over either way.

status and serverCode are separate fields on purpose. A match has a server from the moment it is made, so "a server exists" is not the same question as "the match has started".

docs.title: What decides a roster
docs.text:
Two rules. Failing them is a real outcome: those players stay in the queue rather than being handed a bad match.

  • Teams must be within max_team_elo_gap average Elo of each other.
  • Two players are not put against each other again within rematch_cooldown.

One repeated pairing rejects the whole roster, so (a+b vs c+d) blocks (a+b vs c+e). Swapping one team-mate still leaves a and b facing c a second time.

Parties are never split across teams. Within those constraints, the longest-waiting players are matched first and teams are balanced on Elo. Every number here is in [matchmaking] in config.toml.

docs.text:

docs.title: Self-hosting
docs.text: A real deployment is one container, one Postgres, and a reverse proxy. Nothing else is required.

docs.title: Build and run
docs.text:
cd website
docker build -t peekseek .
docker run --env-file .env -p 8000:8000 peekseek

The build context is website/, not the repository root

The Dockerfile does COPY requirements.txt . and COPY src ./src, both relative to website/. Building from the repository root fails. If your platform asks separately for a Dockerfile path and a context path, they are website/Dockerfile and website.

The build runs minify.py over public/assets after copying it in, so the image serves compressed CSS and JS while the repository keeps readable source. The compressors are uninstalled in the same layer and never reach the running container.

docs.title: Behind a reverse proxy
docs.text:
The container listens on 8000. Point your proxy at it and terminate TLS there.

Do not set --forwarded-allow-ips=*

Game-server authentication trusts request.client.host, and uvicorn's ProxyHeadersMiddleware rewrites that from X-Forwarded-For whenever the peer is in the allowed list. With *, anyone hitting the container can set X-Forwarded-For to an allow-listed address and pass the /server/v1/* IP check with no other access.

The shipped CMD scopes it to Docker's private ranges, so only the proxy's own hop is trusted:

--forwarded-allow-ips=172.16.0.0/12,10.0.0.0/8,192.168.0.0/16

If your proxy reaches the container from outside those ranges, narrow the list to your proxy's address. Do not widen it.

docs.title: Database
docs.text:
Point DB at Postgres. The schema builds itself on startup: create_all adds missing tables, then addMissingColumns adds columns the models have gained, printing each ALTER as it runs.

There is no migration tool and no migration step. Dropping, renaming or retyping a column is not covered and has to be done by hand. See Architecture for what that trade buys.

Back the database up yourself. Nothing in the application does it for you.

docs.title: First run
docs.text:
Two bootstraps exist because a brand-new database cannot be used without them, and neither should stay set.

# Grants admin to one account, creating it if it has never logged in.
BOOTSTRAP_ADMIN_STEAM64=76561198000000000

# Allow-lists game servers: address=region,address=region
BOOTSTRAP_SERVERS=203.0.113.10=paris,203.0.113.11=utah

Every /server/v1/* route returns 401 to an address not in AuthorizedServers, and nothing in the site adds one, so without BOOTSTRAP_SERVERS no game server can ever talk to your instance. Regions come from [regions.names] in config.toml. Addresses already present are left alone, so changing a region here does not overwrite the stored one.

Unset both once they have done their job.

docs.title: Connecting a game server
docs.text:
1. Put the compiled plugin in the server's Rocket/Plugins/<name>/.
  2. Point its configuration at your site's base URL.
  3. Add the server's public IP to BOOTSTRAP_SERVERS, with a region that exists in [regions.names].
  4. Restart the site once so the allow-list entry is created.

The server then polls GET /server/v1/session and the match lifecycle takes over.

Plugin configuration is XML on the server, not in this repository

RocketMod writes each plugin's config file on first load. A new configuration field is not picked up by editing the repository; it has to be added to the live XML on the server, or the file deleted so the plugin regenerates it.

docs.title: Multiple environments
docs.text:
One image serves all of them. Three environment variables override the [app] block in config.toml:

Variable Overrides DOMAIN [app].domain, the public hostname with no scheme PROTOCOL [app].protocol BUILD [app].build, the label the site shows

A staging environment should also leave BOT_TOKEN, LOG_WEBHOOK and QUEUE_LOG_CHANNEL unset. Every one of those callers no-ops on an empty value, so staging can never DM real players or post into production Discord channels. That is the mechanism, not a convention, and it is worth preserving.

docs.title: What PeekSeek itself runs on
docs.text:
Dokploy, with Traefik in front, on a single host. Nothing in the application depends on that, and any Docker host will do.

Two lessons from running it that are cheaper to read than to rediscover:

  • Never let two applications claim the same hostname. Traefik will hold two routers with the same rule, pick one deterministically, and a redeploy can flip which one wins. A healthy container and a 502 at the same time usually means this.
  • A valid certificate proves nothing about your backend. Traefik answers the ACME challenge itself and never touches the container, so a fresh certificate alongside a 502 is exactly the signature of a live router pointed at a dead service.
